title: Complexity Is Not in the Eye of the Beholder
author: Stefan Norrvall
summary: Stefan Norrvall of Synexia argues against the idea that organisational complexity depends on who is looking at it. He replaces the loaded word with structural load, meaning the operational, coordination, integrative and environmental work that an organisation must absorb through roles, platforms, contracts or other mechanisms. His central claim is that an observer decides whether a structural shortfall is found, not whether it exists. He separates understanding from authority, since people can fully grasp a conflict yet lack any legitimate means to resolve it. Using a track-maintenance parable about a supervisor who quietly over-lubricated a curve, he shows why recording and handover fixes are different from asking who can authorise a departure from a standard. He ends with a three-question test for any decision that keeps returning to the same meeting: who understands it, what carries it, and who can change that arrangement.
points: Structural load is the work an arrangement must accommodate, and it exists whether or not any observer notices it, so it has to be designed for.
Understanding a problem does not confer authority to fix it, so more capability development cannot close a shortfall that is really a missing authority or mechanism.
Work that is left off the organisation chart migrates into shadow structure and induced load, which shows up as latency, risk and burnout.
Escalation only helps if it reaches a role able to resolve the condition, because passing a conflict through senior meetings creates no new authority.
A strong diagnosis makes a discriminating, testable claim, for example that adding operational capacity should leave an unarbitrated decision class unresolved.
quotes: Structural load doesn’t come into existence because an observer finds the work difficult, and it doesn’t disappear because another observer finds it easy. It has to be designed for.
Changing the organisation chart does not remove the work. The design question is what absorbs its load, and who can change that arrangement when it stops fitting.
An organisation can contain all the knowledge required to recognise a problem while lacking the authority or mechanisms required to resolve it.
Escalation is useful only if it reaches a role able to resolve that condition. Passing the same conflict through increasingly senior meetings does not create the missing authority.
You can send someone on every sense-making programme on offer; it won’t give them authority their role doesn’t hold.
Finding the shortfall may take unusual insight. Establishing it takes evidence that others can examine. Either way, the shortfall was there before anyone found it.

Pick one decision that keeps returning to the same meeting, and ask three questions of it. Who understands it? What actually carries it now: a role, a rule, a platform, or someone’s goodwill? Who has the authority to change that arrangement?
